prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We investigate the evolution of binary fractions in star clusters using N-body models of up to 100000 stars. Primordial binary frequencies in these models range from 5% to 50%. Simulations are performed with the NBODY4 code and include a full mass spectrum of stars, stellar evolution, binary evolution and the tidal field of the Galaxy. We find that the overall binary fraction of a cluster almost always remains close to the primordial value, except at late times when a cluster is near dissolution. A critical exception occurs in the central regions where we observe a marked increase in binary fraction with time -- a simulation starting with 100000 stars and 5% binaries reached a core binary frequency as high as 40% at the end of the core-collapse phase (occurring at 16 Gyr with ~20000 stars remaining). Binaries are destroyed in the core by a variety of processes as a cluster evolves, but the combination of mass-segregation and creation of new binaries in exchange interactions produces the observed increase in relative number. We also find that binaries are cycled into and out of cluster cores in a manner that is analogous to convection in stars. For models of 100000 stars we show that the evolution of the core-radius up to the end of the initial phase of core-collapse is not affected by the exact value of the primordial binary frequency (for frequencies of 10% or less). We discuss the ramifications of our results for the likely primordial binary content of globular clusters.

outputs.L1: We investigate the evolution of binary fractions in star clusters using N-body models containing up to 100,000 stars. The primordial binary frequencies in these models range from 5% to 50%. The simulations are performed with the NBODY4 code and include a full stellar mass spectrum, stellar evolution, binary evolution, and the tidal field of the Galaxy. We find that the overall binary fraction of a cluster almost always remains close to its primordial value, except at late times when the cluster is near dissolution. A critical exception occurs in the central regions, where we observe a marked increase in the binary fraction over time: a simulation beginning with 100,000 stars and 5% binaries reached a core binary frequency as high as 40% at the end of the core-collapse phase, which occurred at 16 Gyr with approximately 20,000 stars remaining. Although binaries are destroyed in the core through a variety of processes as a cluster evolves, the combination of mass segregation and the creation of new binaries through exchange interactions produces the observed increase in their relative number. We also find that binaries are cycled into and out of cluster cores in a manner analogous to convection in stars. For models of 100,000 stars, we show that the evolution of the core radius up to the end of the initial phase of core collapse is not affected by the exact value of the primordial binary frequency, for frequencies of 10% or less. We discuss the implications of our results for the likely primordial binary content of globular clusters.
outputs.L2:
Using N-body simulations containing as many as 100,000 stars, we study how binary-star fractions change over time in star clusters. The initial, or primordial, binary proportions in the models span 5% to 50%. The calculations are carried out with the NBODY4 code and incorporate a complete stellar mass range, stellar evolution, binary evolution, and the Milky Way’s tidal influence.

Our results show that a cluster’s total binary fraction generally stays near its starting value, except during the late stages when the cluster is close to dissolving. However, the central parts of clusters behave differently: there, the binary fraction rises substantially over time. In one model that began with 100,000 stars and a 5% binary fraction, the binary frequency in the core increased to about 40% by the end of the core-collapse stage, which took place at 16 Gyr when roughly 20,000 stars were still present.

Although several mechanisms destroy binaries in the core as the cluster evolves, the observed growth in their relative abundance results from the combined effects of mass segregation and the formation of additional binaries through exchange encounters. We further find that binaries move repeatedly into and out of cluster cores in a way resembling convection inside stars. For 100,000-star models, the development of the core radius up to the conclusion of the initial core-collapse phase is insensitive to the precise primordial binary fraction, provided that fraction is 10% or lower. We consider what these findings imply for the probable original binary-star populations of globular clusters.
outputs.L3:
The study uses detailed N-body simulations containing up to 100,000 stars to investigate how binary fractions evolve over time in star clusters. By following the dynamical evolution of clusters with different initial binary populations, the study examines both the global binary fraction of the cluster and the binary fraction within the dense central core.

One of the main findings is that the overall binary fraction of a cluster generally remains close to its primordial, or initial, value for most of the cluster’s lifetime. Significant changes in the global binary fraction typically occur only when the cluster is nearing dissolution, at which point the preferential loss of single stars or binaries can noticeably alter the cluster-wide ratio.

In contrast, the binary fraction in the cluster core can evolve much more dramatically. The simulations show that the core binary fraction may increase substantially over time, in some cases reaching values as high as 40%. This means that even if the cluster as a whole retains a binary fraction similar to its initial value, the central region can become strongly enriched in binary systems.

The increase in the core binary fraction is mainly driven by dynamical processes. Mass segregation causes more massive objects, including many binaries, to sink toward the cluster center. In addition, exchange interactions in the dense core can create or preserve binaries by replacing lower-mass companions with more massive stars. These processes can outweigh the destruction of binaries through close encounters, leading to a net increase in the number of binaries in the core.

For the largest models considered, containing 100,000 stars, the study finds that low primordial binary frequencies—10% or less—do not significantly influence the evolution of the core radius before the end of the initial core-collapse phase. In other words, when the initial binary population is modest, binaries are not abundant enough to provide sufficient dynamical energy to noticeably delay or alter early core contraction.
outputs.L4:
This study investigates the dynamical evolution of binary stars in dense stellar systems by means of direct N-body simulations performed with the NBODY4 code. The simulations follow star clusters containing as many as 100,000 stars and include a range of initial conditions, particularly different primordial binary fractions. In addition to gravitational interactions between single stars and binaries, the models incorporate the effects of stellar evolution, binary evolution, and the external tidal field of the Galaxy. This combination allows the simulations to trace not only the global evolution of clusters, but also the changing properties of their central regions, where stellar encounters are most frequent.

A central aim of the work is to determine how the binary fraction changes over time and how that evolution depends on the initial binary content of the cluster. The results show that, when measured over the cluster as a whole, the binary fraction generally remains relatively close to its primordial value for much of the cluster lifetime. Although binaries may be destroyed, altered, or ejected through dynamical encounters and stellar evolution, these processes do not usually produce large changes in the global binary fraction.

The situation is very different in cluster cores. Because binaries are typically more massive than single stars, they tend to sink toward the cluster center through mass segregation. Once concentrated in the core, binaries take part in frequent dynamical encounters, including binary-single and binary-binary interactions. Exchange encounters can replace lower-mass binary components with more massive stars, while hard binaries tend to become harder and can act as an important energy source for the cluster. As a result, the core binary fraction can increase substantially, in some cases becoming much larger than the overall cluster binary fraction.

These findings have important implications for the interpretation of observed binary populations in globular clusters. A high binary fraction in a cluster core does not necessarily mean that the entire cluster was born with an extremely high binary content; it may instead reflect the long-term effects of mass segregation and dynamical processing. Conversely, the present-day global binary fraction can provide constraints on the primordial binary fraction and on the cluster’s dynamical history. The study therefore emphasizes that observations of binary stars, especially when core and global populations are distinguished, offer a valuable tool for understanding the formation, evolution, and long-term stability of globular clusters.
outputs.L5:
**Primordial Simulations and the Birth of Galaxies**

Primordial simulations help scientists explore the earliest stages of the universe, long before modern galaxies took shape. By using powerful computers, researchers can recreate conditions shortly after the Big Bang, when matter was spread across space in a hot, dense, and nearly uniform state. Over time, tiny fluctuations in this primordial matter grew under the force of gravity, eventually forming the first stars, gas clouds, and galaxies.

These simulations are essential because the early universe cannot be observed directly in full detail. They allow astronomers to test theories about how dark matter, hydrogen gas, and radiation interacted during cosmic history. In a typical galaxy formation simulation, dark matter first gathers into large invisible halos. Gas then falls into these halos, cools, and begins forming stars. As more stars are born, they release energy, metals, and radiation, changing the structure and evolution of the young galaxy.

Studying primordial galaxy formation also helps explain why galaxies today have such different shapes and sizes. Some became large spiral galaxies, while others formed as smaller dwarf galaxies or massive elliptical systems. Simulations show that mergers, star formation, supernova explosions, and black holes all played important roles in shaping these systems.

As technology improves, primordial simulations are becoming more accurate and detailed. They give scientists a powerful window into the ancient universe and help answer one of astronomy’s biggest questions: how did the first galaxies emerge from the darkness after the Big Bang?

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for an astrophysics paper about N-body simulations of binary star fractions in globular clusters, including primordial binary frequencies, NBODY4, stellar/binary evolution, Galactic tides, core binary fraction growth, and implications for globular clusters.
counterfactuals.output:
We present a suite of direct \(N\)-body simulations of globular clusters designed to investigate the dynamical evolution of binary-star populations over a Hubble time. The models are initialized with a range of primordial binary frequencies and evolved using **NBODY4**, including two-body relaxation, strong few-body encounters, stellar and binary evolution, and the effects of the Galactic tidal field. We follow the global and radial evolution of the binary fraction, with particular emphasis on the cluster core, where mass segregation and dynamical processing strongly modify the initially imposed binary population. 

Our simulations show that, although binaries are efficiently disrupted in dense environments, the core binary fraction generally increases with time as surviving binaries segregate inward and single stars are preferentially depleted through evaporation and tidal stripping. The magnitude of this growth depends sensitively on the primordial binary frequency, cluster concentration, encounter rate, and binary binding-energy distribution. Models with higher initial binary fractions retain dynamically significant binary populations capable of providing an important internal energy source, delaying core collapse and altering the long-term structural evolution of the cluster. 

These results demonstrate that present-day core binary fractions in globular clusters are not simple tracers of primordial binary content, but instead reflect the combined effects of stellar evolution, binary interactions, relaxation, and Galactic tides. Our findings provide a framework for interpreting observed binary fractions in Galactic globular clusters and highlight the importance of realistic binary populations in modeling cluster dynamics, core evolution, and the survival of globular clusters over cosmological timescales.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a study investigating how binary fractions evolve in star clusters using direct N-body models with up to 100,000 stars and primordial binary fractions from 5% to 50%.
counterfactuals.output:
The study used direct N-body simulations of realistic star clusters containing up to **100,000 stars**, with **primordial binary fractions** ranging from **5% to 50%**, to examine how binary populations change dynamically over a cluster lifetime.

Key results:

- **Binary fractions evolve strongly with time.** Many primordial binaries are destroyed, especially early on, through close encounters with other stars and binaries.

- **Soft binaries are preferentially disrupted.** Wide, weakly bound binaries are easily broken apart in dense cluster environments, while hard, tightly bound binaries tend to survive and may become even harder through encounters.

- **Cluster density matters.** Dense clusters process binaries more efficiently, destroying a larger fraction of their initial binary population. Lower-density clusters retain more binaries.

- **The observed binary fraction is not the primordial fraction.** Even clusters born with high binary fractions can evolve to much lower present-day binary fractions, meaning current observations cannot be interpreted directly without accounting for dynamical evolution.

- **Binary fractions vary with radius.** Binaries tend to become more centrally concentrated because they are, on average, more massive than single stars and sink toward the cluster core through mass segregation.

- **Binaries affect cluster structure.** Surviving hard binaries act as an internal energy source through dynamical interactions, helping to delay or regulate core collapse and influencing the size and evolution of the cluster core.

- **Initial binary fraction leaves a detectable imprint.** Models with higher primordial binary fractions generally retain more binaries and show different core evolution than models with fewer initial binaries, although dynamical destruction reduces the differences over time.

Overall, the study shows that binary populations in star clusters are shaped by a combination of **initial conditions, stellar evolution, mass segregation, and dynamical encounters**. Present-day binary fractions—especially in globular clusters—are therefore the outcome of long-term dynamical processing rather than simple reflections of how many binaries the clusters formed with.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise journal-style abstract describing results from NBODY4 simulations showing that cluster-wide binary fractions stay near primordial values while core binary fractions increase due to mass segregation and exchange interactions.
counterfactuals.output: We present results from direct NBODY4 simulations of star clusters with primordial binary populations, focusing on the evolution of binary fractions in the cluster as a whole and in the dynamically active core. The simulations show that the global binary fraction remains close to its primordial value over many relaxation times, despite ongoing binary disruption and stellar escape. In contrast, the core binary fraction increases substantially with time. This enhancement is driven primarily by mass segregation, which concentrates the typically more massive binary systems toward the cluster centre, and by exchange interactions that preferentially replace lower-mass companions with more massive stars, further increasing the central binary abundance. Binary destruction in strong encounters partly offsets this growth but does not prevent the development of a binary-rich core. These results demonstrate that core binary fractions are not reliable tracers of the initial cluster-wide binary content without accounting for dynamical evolution, and they highlight the importance of direct N-body modelling for interpreting observed binary populations in dense stellar systems.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a scientific abstract based on simulations of star clusters that include a full stellar mass spectrum, stellar evolution, binary evolution, and the Galactic tidal field, focusing on binary destruction, creation, and cycling in cluster cores.
counterfactuals.output:
We present simulations of dense star clusters that follow the long-term dynamical evolution of a full stellar mass spectrum in the presence of stellar evolution, binary evolution, and the Galactic tidal field. The models are designed to investigate the coupled processes of binary destruction, binary formation, and binary cycling in cluster cores, where mass segregation, close encounters, and stellar evolution drive rapid changes in the binary population.

Our results show that the core binary population is not determined solely by the primordial binary fraction, but by a continuous balance between dynamical processing and replenishment. Soft binaries are efficiently destroyed through encounters, especially during early cluster evolution and during phases of enhanced central density. Hard binaries, in contrast, generally survive and act as an internal energy source, delaying or reversing core contraction through superelastic encounters. New binaries are produced dynamically through exchange interactions, three-body encounters, and interactions involving compact remnants, while stellar and binary evolution modify orbital separations, component masses, and survival probabilities.

We find that binary cycling is a generic feature of evolved cluster cores: binaries are segregated into the core, hardened or exchanged through encounters, ejected to larger radii or from the cluster, and replaced by newly segregated or dynamically formed systems. This cycle is strongly regulated by the Galactic tidal field, which removes weakly bound stars and binaries, alters the cluster mass function, and accelerates the depletion of loosely bound systems. Compact remnants, particularly white dwarfs, neutron stars, and stellar-mass black holes, play a disproportionate role in reshaping the binary population through exchanges and energetic interactions.

These simulations demonstrate that the observed binary content of cluster cores is the product of a complex, time-dependent interplay between stellar evolution, binary evolution, relaxation, and tidal stripping. The core binary fraction, orbital-parameter distribution, and incidence of exotic binaries therefore provide sensitive diagnostics of a cluster’s dynamical history and its interaction with the Galactic environment.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a research-paper abstract explaining how primordial binary frequency affects core-collapse evolution in 100,000-star cluster models, noting that low initial binary fractions do not significantly change core-radius evolution before core collapse.
counterfactuals.output: We present a numerical study of how the primordial binary fraction influences the dynamical evolution of core collapse in star cluster models containing 100,000 stars. Using direct or statistically equivalent collisional cluster simulations, we compare models initialized with different fractions of primordial binaries while keeping the global cluster structure and stellar population fixed. We find that primordial binaries affect core evolution primarily through binary-mediated energy generation in the dense central region. At sufficiently high initial binary fractions, binary–single and binary–binary encounters provide an internal heat source that slows contraction, delays core collapse, and can produce a larger post-collapse core radius. In contrast, models with low initial binary fractions show core-radius evolution that is nearly indistinguishable from single-star-dominated models during the pre-collapse phase. In these cases, the number of primordial binaries is insufficient to generate enough dynamical heating before the onset of deep core contraction, so the cluster proceeds toward core collapse on a relaxation-driven timescale similar to that of models without significant binary populations. The results indicate that the primordial binary fraction is a key control parameter for the timing and severity of core collapse only once it exceeds the threshold needed for binary burning to compete with gravothermal contraction. These findings emphasize that modest binary populations do not necessarily alter early core evolution, while rich primordial binary populations can substantially regulate the long-term structural evolution of dense star clusters.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
